facts: Research-based personas are shareable profiles of user groups with similar behavior and needs.
Personas keep design choices connected to evidence instead of isolated assumptions.
Personas also present research findings so other people can understand and share them.
User needs are usually higher-level and more stable than individual interface requests.
Teams turn user needs into user stories that describe features and content for those needs.

keyTerms.df: A research-based persona is a profile built from observed user-group patterns and used to guide design decisions.
keyTerms.eg: A team summarizes repeated behavior and shared needs into one profile for a support-focused user group.
keyTerms.mi: A persona is just a fictional character invented to make screens feel more human.
keyTerms.cx: It comes from research patterns, not imagination, so it organizes evidence rather than decoration.

keyTerms.df: User needs are broader requirements that describe what people require over time, not a single screen request.
keyTerms.eg: Someone who must quickly compare account details needs a stable way to find and check information.
keyTerms.mi: A user need is the same thing as a request for one button or one layout change.
keyTerms.cx: A button request can change quickly, while a need stays at the level of the underlying requirement.

keyTerms.df: User stories are feature and content descriptions written to address identified user needs within a team.
keyTerms.eg: A story might describe a page element that helps people review information they need repeatedly.
keyTerms.mi: A user story is only a marketing phrase and has no link to evidence or needs.
keyTerms.cx: The story should be tied back to the underlying need so its purpose can be checked.

scenario.su: A design team is comparing a persona profile, a list of user needs, and several drafted user stories before approving a new service page. They must choose which items belong together while keeping the work connected to research evidence.
scenario.ma: The persona shows shared behavior and needs, the needs list says people want stable access to account information, and one story proposes a quick-filter feature for that need. The team must decide whether the story belongs with that need and keep the linkage visible in the design record.

mc.q: A workshop shows a profile built from shared behavior, alongside a page request for a single button. Which statement best distinguishes the profile from the request using the evidence presented?
op: The profile is a user story, while the button request is a user need.
The profile is a single interface request, while the button request is a stable need.
The profile is only a visual mockup, while the button request is the research finding.
The profile is a research-based persona, while the button request is an individual interface request.
mc.ex: The evidence describes a shareable profile built from group behavior and needs, which matches a research-based persona. The button request is narrower and more specific, so it is an individual interface request rather than the broader profile.

mc.q: A planning board shows a stable requirement for account information, plus a drafted feature note for faster filtering. What should be linked so later review can check whether the requirement is being met?
op: The feature note should replace the user need because it is more detailed.
The feature note should stay linked to the underlying user need.
The persona should be linked only to the visual style of the page.
The user need should be rewritten as a mockup and detached from the feature note.
mc.ex: The feature note is a user story, and it should remain linked to the underlying need so the team can evaluate whether the need is met. Detaching it would hide that relationship, and the visual style alone does not track need fulfillment.

facts: Electric potential is electric potential energy per unit charge at a point.
Potential difference is the work per unit charge required between two points.
Only potential differences change electrostatic work and energy, not an absolute value.
An electric field points toward decreasing electric potential in space.
Comparing potential values helps predict how charges and energy will change.

keyTerms.df: Electric potential is a scalar quantity describing potential energy available per unit charge at a point.
keyTerms.eg: A point beside a charged plate can have a higher electric potential than a point farther away.
keyTerms.mi: Electric potential is the total energy stored in the entire charged object.
keyTerms.cx: That confuses a per-charge quantity with a total quantity; electric potential describes energy per unit charge, not the whole system.

keyTerms.df: Potential difference is the change in electric potential between two points and describes work per unit charge.
keyTerms.eg: Moving a charge from one marked point to another across a gap involves a specific potential difference.
keyTerms.mi: Potential difference is the same as the electric potential at a single point.
keyTerms.cx: A single-point value is not a difference; the quantity here compares two locations and ties directly to work per unit charge.

keyTerms.df: An electric field is a vector quantity that indicates the direction a positive test charge would experience decreasing electric potential.
keyTerms.eg: On a sketch, field arrows point from the higher-potential region toward the lower-potential region.
keyTerms.mi: The electric field points toward increasing electric potential because charges move where potential is larger.
keyTerms.cx: That reverses the relationship; the field direction matches decreasing potential, not increasing potential.

scenario.su: A diagram shows two nearby points labeled 12 V and 7 V, with an arrow drawn between them and a note about a positive charge. A student must decide which way the electric field points while keeping the energy change per charge consistent with the labels.
scenario.ma: Compare the 12 V and 7 V labels, the arrow between the points, and the note about a positive charge moving through the gap.

mc.q: On a sketch, one point is labeled 9 V and a nearby point is labeled 4 V. Which statement best distinguishes the two quantities by what each compares?
op: Electric potential and potential difference both mean the same total energy stored in the region.
Electric potential is only meaningful when two points are compared, while potential difference is a single-point value.
Potential difference is the field strength at the lower-numbered point, while electric potential is the charge itself.
Electric potential is energy per unit charge at one point, while potential difference compares work per unit charge between two points.
mc.ex: The labels show a single-point value and a two-point comparison, so energy per unit charge matches electric potential and the work-per-charge change matches potential difference. The closest distractor collapses them into one total energy idea, which ignores the distinction between a point value and a difference.

mc.q: A positive charge is moved from a point marked 15 V to a point marked 6 V, and the path is otherwise unspecified. What direction should the electric field be drawn between the points?
op: Perpendicular to the line connecting the two points.
No direction can be determined from the voltage labels.
From the 15 V point toward the 6 V point.
From the 6 V point toward the 15 V point.
mc.ex: The field points in the direction of decreasing electric potential, so the arrow goes from 15 V toward 6 V. The closest distractor reverses that relationship, but increasing potential is the wrong direction for the field here.

facts: A research plan turns a decision need into actionable learning objectives.
A research plan also sets participant choices, tasks, and evidence-capture roles.
A study setup should be rehearsal-ready before participants enter the room.
The team should agree what it wants to learn before choosing study details.
A practice session with a team member can reveal procedure problems early.

keyTerms.df: A research plan is the structured preparation that converts a decision need into specific study aims and roles.
keyTerms.eg: A team frames a checkout-flow question, then lists participant tasks and who records observations.
keyTerms.mi: A research plan is just a rough agenda for the meeting.
keyTerms.cx: It is broader than an agenda because it organizes what must be learned, not only timing.

keyTerms.df: A study setup is the prepared arrangement of tasks, materials, and room conditions for the session.
keyTerms.eg: The prototype is placed so the participant can complete the path without extra assistance.
keyTerms.mi: A study setup can be assembled after participants arrive.
keyTerms.cx: Preparation must be ready in advance because the session depends on a usable arrangement from the start.

keyTerms.df: A practice session is a rehearsal run that checks whether the procedure works smoothly before the real session.
keyTerms.eg: A team member steps through the tasks while the moderator checks timing and note-taking.
keyTerms.mi: A practice session is useful only after real participants have started the study.
keyTerms.cx: The point is to expose procedure problems beforehand, so rehearsal happens before participants arrive.

scenario.su: A product team has a prototype for an account-reset flow and wants to study it with participants tomorrow. The flow has a missing confirmation screen, and the room plan leaves one observer without a clear note-taking role.
scenario.ma: The draft research plan, the prototype screen sequence, and the note about evidence-capture roles are being compared against the room setup sheet and the task script.

mc.q: A team is choosing between two descriptions: one names learning goals, participant tasks, and note-taking roles; the other mainly lists meeting timing. Which description matches a research plan more closely?
op: The description that only names the prototype screens without study roles.
The description that mainly schedules the meeting blocks and speaker order.
The description that focuses on post-session reporting instead of preparation.
The description that turns a decision need into learning objectives, participants, tasks, and roles.
mc.ex: The research plan is the structure that converts a decision need into learning objectives, participants, tasks, and evidence-capture roles. The timing-only description is closer to a schedule, not a research plan.

mc.q: A moderator notices the prototype fails at the final step, one observer has no note-taking role, and the team has a rehearsal with a colleague before tomorrow. Which action best fits the preparation described?
op: Skip rehearsal and let the participant discover procedure problems first.
Keep the broken end-to-end flow as it is so reactions stay natural.
Start the session and adjust the procedure after the first participant leaves.
Run through the test tasks in a practice session before participants arrive.
mc.ex: A practice session helps expose procedure problems before participants arrive, which fits the rehearsal described. Waiting for the first participant to expose issues would miss the preparation purpose.

facts: Homeostasis maintains stable internal conditions through negative-feedback loops.
A set point is the physiological value around which normal range fluctuates.
A feedback loop includes a sensor, a control center, and an effector.
The sensor detects deviation and sends information to the control center.
The effector produces a response that reverses the deviation toward the set point.

keyTerms.df: Homeostasis is the maintenance of stable internal conditions within a living system.
keyTerms.eg: A body keeping internal conditions steady despite a small change shows homeostasis.
keyTerms.mi: Homeostasis means internal conditions stay exactly fixed with no fluctuation.
keyTerms.cx: Internal conditions can vary around a stable target while still showing homeostasis.

keyTerms.df: A set point is the physiological value around which a normal range fluctuates.
keyTerms.eg: A temperature target that the body returns toward reflects a set point.
keyTerms.mi: A set point is the widest possible range of values that remains healthy.
keyTerms.cx: A set point is a central value, not the entire range around it.

keyTerms.df: A feedback loop is a coordinated system of detection, control, and response.
keyTerms.eg: A detector, comparator, and responding unit working together form a feedback loop.
keyTerms.mi: A feedback loop is only the final response that changes the condition.
keyTerms.cx: The loop also requires sensing and control, not just the response itself.

scenario.su: A student compares a note that shows internal conditions drifting upward with a sketch of a regulator that sends a corrective response. Time is limited, so the student must decide whether the control pattern describes homeostasis or only a fixed target value.
scenario.ma: The first note records a deviation from a usual value and a response that pushes the value back. The second sketch labels a sensor, a control center, and an effector, with arrows showing the response moving conditions toward the usual value.

mc.q: A measured value rises above its usual level, and a response pushes it back toward the usual level. Which statement best matches the relationship between homeostasis and set point in this situation?
op: Homeostasis is the target value itself, while the set point is the corrective response that changes the value.
Homeostasis is only the detector that notices change, while the set point is the response unit.
Homeostasis and set point both mean the same fixed value with no fluctuation.
Homeostasis is the negative-feedback process that reverses the deviation, while the set point is the usual target value.
mc.ex: The deviation is reversed by a negative-feedback process, which fits homeostasis, and the usual target value is the set point. The closest distractor confuses the target value with the corrective response, but those are different roles.

mc.q: A diagram labels a detector, a comparator, and a responding unit, and the final arrows show the variable moving back toward its usual value. Which sequence names those parts in order?
op: control center, effector, sensor
sensor, control center, effector
sensor, effector, control center
effector, sensor, control center
mc.ex: A feedback loop is built from sensing, control, and response, so the detector is the sensor, the comparator is the control center, and the responding unit is the effector. The closest distractor swaps the order, but the roles are not interchangeable.

facts: File I/O lets a program read information from files and write information into files.
A file is accessed by opening it, working with its contents, and closing it.
open() returns a file object that the program then reads from or writes to.
read() reads the entire contents of a file and returns one single string.
readline() returns the next single line, while readlines() returns a list of every line.

keyTerms.df: File I/O is the use of files as external containers for program input and output.
keyTerms.eg: A script reads a saved note file, updates its contents, and writes a new copy.
keyTerms.mi: File I/O means the program only prints text to the screen.
keyTerms.cx: File I/O concerns files as data sources and destinations, not just display output.

keyTerms.df: open() is the operation that creates a file object for later reading or writing.
keyTerms.eg: Calling open() before using a text file lets code access its stored contents.
keyTerms.mi: open() itself reads every line from the file immediately.
keyTerms.cx: open() only prepares the file object; reading happens later with methods like read().

keyTerms.df: readlines() is a file method that gathers every line into a list structure.
keyTerms.eg: When a text file has several short lines, readlines() can collect them all at once.
keyTerms.mi: readlines() returns one long string with all the text merged together.
keyTerms.cx: readlines() produces a list of separate lines, unlike read() which returns one string.

scenario.su: A teammate opens a text file that stores three course notes, but the script must preserve each line separately. The file contains a blank line in the middle, and the program must choose one read method before a later write step.
scenario.ma: The notes show three visible lines, a blank line between them, and a requirement to keep line breaks distinct when the program reviews the file. A developer must decide whether to use read(), readline(), or readlines() before writing a cleaned copy.

mc.q: A programmer opens a text file and needs a result that keeps each line separate for later counting. Which behavior matches the method shown in the record with several lines preserved?
op: readlines() returns a list with every line of the file.
read() returns the next single line only.
readline() returns the entire contents as one string.
open() returns the file contents immediately.
mc.ex: The record with several preserved lines matches readlines(), because it collects every line into a list. The closest distractor is read(), but that method returns one single string, not separate lines.

mc.q: A note says the program must load the whole text at once before cleaning spaces, and the saved file should keep the original content available as one block. Which file behavior fits that observation?
op: read() returns the entire contents of a file as one string.
readline() returns every line as a list.
open() closes the file after the call finishes.
readlines() returns only the first line.
mc.ex: The observation matches read(), which reads the whole file and returns one string. The closest distractor is readlines(), but that method returns a list of lines rather than one combined string.

facts: A function is a named, reusable block of code that runs only when called.
Variables created inside a function are local to that call and do not persist globally.
The def keyword introduces a function name, parentheses, and a colon before an indented body.
Variable scope is the part of a program where a variable can be accessed.
A variable created outside any function has global scope and can be accessed anywhere.

keyTerms.df: A function is a named block of code defined to be reused when called, not when written.
keyTerms.eg: A def block that prints a message only after a later call shows a function.
keyTerms.mi: Any indented code is automatically a function, even without def or a call.
keyTerms.cx: Indentation alone does not make a function; the defining marker and later call are both required.

keyTerms.df: Variable scope is the region of a program where a variable name can be accessed successfully.
keyTerms.eg: A name used inside one function but not outside it demonstrates limited variable scope.
keyTerms.mi: Scope means a variable changes value every time it is used in a program.
keyTerms.cx: Scope concerns where a name is reachable, not how often its value changes.

keyTerms.df: Global scope describes a variable created outside functions that remains accessible throughout the program.
keyTerms.eg: A name defined before any function and read inside another block shows global scope.
keyTerms.mi: A global variable can be accessed only inside the function where it was created.
keyTerms.cx: That reverses the idea of global scope; outside-function names are reachable across the program.

scenario.su: A debugging notebook shows a def block named score_total and a later print statement that uses score. The notebook also notes that score is created inside the function, while limit is created before the function, and the team must choose which name a later line can read without changing the code.
scenario.ma: Compare the function header with its indented body, the note beside score saying 'created inside', and the separate line where limit is defined before def. Decide which name can be accessed later outside the function while the other stays limited to one call.

mc.q: A script shows a def line with parentheses and a colon, followed by an indented block. Which statement best matches how that structure behaves compared with the code above it?
op: It defines a reusable function that runs only after a later call.
It copies the indented code into every earlier line automatically.
It creates a global variable that is available immediately everywhere.
It makes every line in the file run only inside that block.
mc.ex: The defining pattern is a named block that waits until called, while the nearby distractor confuses definition with immediate execution.

mc.q: After a call finishes, a name assigned inside the function is read on a later line and raises a lookup problem. Which explanation best fits the displayed behavior?
op: The name has global scope because it was created during execution.
The name has local scope inside that call and is not available outside it.
The indented block automatically promotes every name to program-wide access.
The function definition erased the name before the body started.
mc.ex: The assignment inside the function creates a local name for that call only; the nearby distractor wrongly treats creation during execution as global access.

facts: Relative dating orders geological events without assigning numerical ages.
Superposition in undisturbed sedimentary layers places older beds below younger beds.
Cross-cutting features are younger than the rocks or structures they cut.
Inclusions are older than the rock that contains them.
Relative dating compares relationships among layers, cuts, and disruptions to sequence events.

keyTerms.df: Relative dating is a method for arranging geological events by relationships, not by numerical age.
keyTerms.eg: A geologist compares a fault, a lava layer, and sediment beds to order them.
keyTerms.mi: Relative dating means calculating the exact age of each rock layer.
keyTerms.cx: That is incorrect because the method establishes sequence from relationships, not exact numbers.

keyTerms.df: Superposition is the principle that, in an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, lower layers formed earlier than higher layers.
keyTerms.eg: In a flat sediment stack, the lowest mudstone bed predates the sandstone above it.
keyTerms.mi: Superposition says the top layer in a stack is always the oldest.
keyTerms.cx: That reverses the sequence; in undisturbed layers, lower beds are older than higher ones.

keyTerms.df: Cross-cutting describes a feature that disrupts another feature and therefore formed later than what it cuts.
keyTerms.eg: A fracture slicing through several beds must be younger than those beds.
keyTerms.mi: Cross-cutting means the cutting feature must be older because it appears narrower.
keyTerms.cx: Narrowness does not set age; cutting or disruption shows the cutter formed after the cut rock.

scenario.su: A field notebook shows flat sedimentary beds with a narrow fault trace slicing upward through three layers. The team must decide which feature formed first, but no numerical ages are available.
scenario.ma: The notebook sketch shows the fault line crossing the beds, a note that the strata are undisturbed, and a lower shale bed beneath a sandstone bed; students compare the fault trace, the layer order, and the undisturbed sequence.

mc.q: A sketch shows an undisturbed stack of sedimentary beds, with a thin basalt layer inserted near the top and a fault cutting through all beds. Which statement best matches relative dating?
op: The top bed is older than the lower beds because it lies closest to the surface.
The basalt layer must be older than every bed because it is thinner than the others.
The fault is older than the beds because it appears to slice the stack cleanly.
The lowest bed is older than the beds above it, and the fault is younger than every bed it cuts.
mc.ex: Relative dating uses relationships, so lower beds in an undisturbed stack are older, and a cutting fault is younger than the beds it disrupts. The thin basalt layer being inserted does not make it older.

mc.q: A shale bed contains pebbles of sandstone, and a nearby fracture cuts through the shale and pebble-rich layer. With no numerical ages, which interpretation fits the records best?
op: The pebble-rich layer must be the youngest because it is inside another rock.
The shale is older than the pebbles because it surrounds them.
The fracture is older than the shale because it appears in a narrow line.
The pebbles are older than the shale that contains them, and the fracture is younger than both.
mc.ex: Inclusions are older than the rock that contains them, so the sandstone pebbles predate the shale. The fracture is younger than the layers it cuts, whereas being narrow does not make it older.

facts: Gauss's law links net electric flux through a closed surface to enclosed charge.
A Gaussian surface helps when symmetry simplifies field magnitude or direction on it.
Zero enclosed charge means zero net flux through the closed surface.
Zero net flux does not require the electric field to vanish everywhere.
The enclosed charge determines the flux, while surface shape alone does not.

keyTerms.df: A field relation that connects total electric flux across a closed surface with charge inside it.
keyTerms.eg: A spherical surface around a charged object lets the enclosed charge set the net flux.
keyTerms.mi: It says the electric field must be the same everywhere on any closed surface.
keyTerms.cx: The law ties flux to enclosed charge, not uniform field strength over the whole surface.

keyTerms.df: A chosen closed surface used because symmetry can make the field easier to evaluate there.
keyTerms.eg: A symmetric closed surface can make the field direction or magnitude simple to track.
keyTerms.mi: It is a physical shell that changes the charge distribution by itself.
keyTerms.cx: It is only a mathematical surface for analysis, so it does not alter the charges.

keyTerms.df: A surface that fully encloses a region, allowing flux to be compared with charge inside.
keyTerms.eg: A surface surrounding the region can be used to relate inside charge to outside flux.
keyTerms.mi: If the enclosed charge is zero, the electric field must be zero at every point.
keyTerms.cx: Zero enclosed charge fixes the net flux only, while the field can still vary across the surface.

scenario.su: A student compares a field map for a symmetric object and a note that the net enclosed charge is zero. They must decide whether the net flux must vanish and whether the field must vanish everywhere, but the surface choice must stay closed.
scenario.ma: The packet includes a spherical surface sketch, a charge tally showing zero enclosed charge, and field arrows that are larger on one side than the other. The student must compare the charge tally with the arrow pattern and choose whether the flux conclusion or the everywhere-zero-field conclusion fits the records.

mc.q: A closed surface surrounds a region where the charge tally is zero, but the field arrows on the surface vary in size and direction. Which statement matches the observation most closely?
op: The electric field must be zero everywhere because the enclosed charge is zero.
The net flux is zero, yet the electric field can still vary across the surface.
The net flux must be nonzero because the field arrows are not uniform.
The surface cannot be used because varying arrows break the rule.
mc.ex: Zero enclosed charge fixes the net flux, not the field at every point. The closest distractor is that zero charge forces the field to vanish everywhere, but the field can still be nonuniform.

mc.q: A symmetric closed surface is drawn around a charged region, and the field direction is simple on that surface. Which interpretation best fits why that surface is chosen?
op: It is useful only when the field is zero everywhere on the surface.
It is useful because symmetry can make the field magnitude or direction simple there.
It is useful because the surface itself creates the electric field pattern.
It is useful because any closed surface automatically makes charge easier to count.
mc.ex: Symmetry can simplify the field on a Gaussian surface, making flux evaluation manageable. The closest distractor is that any closed surface automatically simplifies charge counting, but the special advantage comes from symmetry, not closure alone.

facts: Rigid lithospheric plates move above mantle rock that remains solid yet flows slowly.
Heat transfer within the mantle sustains convection and helps drive plate motion.
Upward mantle flow at ocean ridges helps form new lithosphere.
At convergent boundaries, one plate can be subducted beneath another plate.
Lithosphere and mantle convection together explain how plates diverge and collide.

keyTerms.df: Lithospheric plates are the rigid outer pieces of Earth that move as surface units above weaker deeper material.
keyTerms.eg: A diverging ridge shows lithospheric plates separating while new rock forms below.
keyTerms.mi: Lithospheric plates are soft layers that melt and drift with the mantle.
keyTerms.cx: They are stiff outer slabs, not melted material, and they move over deeper rock that can deform slowly.

keyTerms.df: Mantle convection is slow circulation in heated mantle rock that transfers heat and helps move the outer plates.
keyTerms.eg: Warm mantle rises beneath an ocean ridge while cooler material sinks elsewhere.
keyTerms.mi: Mantle convection means the mantle is liquid and bubbles upward like water.
keyTerms.cx: The mantle remains solid, yet it can flow gradually enough for circulation to continue.

keyTerms.df: Subducted describes a plate descending into the mantle beneath another plate at a convergent boundary.
keyTerms.eg: A convergent margin can show one plate bending downward beneath its neighbor.
keyTerms.mi: Subducted means the two plates scrape sideways and stay at the same depth.
keyTerms.cx: The descending plate moves downward into the mantle rather than sliding past at one level.

scenario.su: Two boundary sketches come from the same map, but the labels are incomplete. One sketch shows plates moving apart above a ridge with upward mantle flow, and the other shows one plate bending beneath another at a margin.
scenario.ma: Students compare the ridge sketch, the bent-down plate sketch, the note that heat transfer sustains mantle convection, and the label that new lithosphere forms where plates diverge; they must match each drawing to the correct boundary process without using outside descriptions.

mc.q: A diagram shows rigid surface plates moving apart above rising mantle rock, while deeper material remains solid but slowly flows. Which description fits that relationship best?
op: The plates are fixed, and only surface erosion makes them appear to move.
The entire mantle is molten, so plates ride on a liquid layer.
Rigid lithospheric plates move above mantle rock that remains solid yet can flow slowly.
The deep rock is rigid, while the surface layer flows like soft clay.
mc.ex: The supported description matches rigid lithospheric plates above solid mantle rock that can still flow slowly. The molten-mantle idea is the closest distractor, but the mantle is described as solid rather than liquid.

mc.q: A cross-section at a convergent boundary shows one plate dipping beneath another, and the map notes a trench beside the contact. Which interpretation best matches that arrangement?
op: One plate is subducted into the mantle beneath another plate.
The crust is thickening only from surface folding, with no downward motion.
Both plates are spreading apart while new lithosphere forms between them.
The plates are sliding past each other at equal depth.
mc.ex: The dipping plate beneath another at a convergent boundary indicates subduction into the mantle. The spreading-apart choice is the closest distractor, but divergence fits ridges, not a descending plate at a convergent margin.

facts: The skeletal system includes bones and cartilage that support the body.
It enables movement, protects organs, produces blood cells, and stores minerals and fat.
Bone is hard, dense connective tissue forming most of the adult skeleton.
Bones provide attachment points that help muscles move the body.
Cartilage is part of the skeletal system, alongside bones, in structural support.

keyTerms.df: The skeletal system is the body framework made of tissues that support, protect, and help movement.
keyTerms.eg: A rib cage and attached cartilage help shield the heart and lungs.
keyTerms.mi: The skeletal system is only a set of rigid parts for standing.
keyTerms.cx: It also includes cartilage and supports movement, protection, blood cell production, and storage.

keyTerms.df: Bone is a hard, dense connective tissue that makes up most adult skeletal structure.
keyTerms.eg: A femur is a bone that contributes to the adult skeleton.
keyTerms.mi: Bone is the soft tissue between muscles and joints.
keyTerms.cx: Bone is the dense connective tissue itself, not a soft padding tissue.

keyTerms.df: Cartilage is a flexible skeletal tissue that works with bones in body support.
keyTerms.eg: Cartilage at joints can be part of the skeletal system's structure.
keyTerms.mi: Cartilage is the same as bone because both are equally hard.
keyTerms.cx: Cartilage is not hard dense connective tissue; it is a flexible supporting tissue.

scenario.su: A lab team examines a torso model showing ribs, shoulder attachments, and flexible joint regions. They must decide which structures belong to the skeletal system while keeping movement and protection in view.
scenario.ma: The model label lists bones and cartilage, and the notes mention muscle attachment points near the ribs and shoulder. A comparison sheet also names organ protection and adult skeleton structure.

mc.q: A model shows a hard, dense structure with muscle attachments, while a nearby flexible tissue is also labeled. Which interpretation best fits the contrast between bone and cartilage?
op: Neither structure belongs to the skeletal system because only organs are shown.
The hard structure is cartilage, and the flexible tissue is bone.
The hard structure is bone, and the flexible tissue is cartilage.
Both labels refer to the same tissue type in different parts of the body.
mc.ex: Bone is the hard, dense connective tissue, while cartilage is the more flexible skeletal tissue. The closest distractor reverses those properties.

mc.q: A student points to ribs, shoulder attachments, and a note about blood cell production, but must choose the best description under a time limit. Which statement matches the observed skeletal roles?
op: Bones are muscle tissue that contracts to move the body directly.
The skeletal system supports the body, helps movement, protects organs, and produces blood cells.
The skeletal system only stores fat and cannot participate in protection.
Cartilage is the main adult skeleton tissue and replaces most bone.
mc.ex: The observed ribs, attachments, and blood cell note fit the skeletal system's support, movement, protection, and production roles. The closest distractor wrongly narrows the system to storage alone.

facts: Price elasticity of demand equals percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price.
Elastic demand means the absolute value of elasticity is greater than one in magnitude.
Necessities often show inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes available nearby.
Close substitutes strongly influence elasticity because easier switching reduces response to price changes.
A larger price change can produce a smaller quantity response when demand is inelastic.

keyTerms.df: Price elasticity measures how quantity demanded responds proportionally to a price change.
keyTerms.eg: If price rises and quantity demanded falls by a larger percentage, price elasticity is high.
keyTerms.mi: Price elasticity measures the total dollars spent after a price change.
keyTerms.cx: It compares percentage changes in quantity demanded and price, not spending levels.

keyTerms.df: Elastic demand describes a demand response where the quantity change proportionally exceeds the price change.
keyTerms.eg: A product with several comparable brands may show elastic demand when price increases.
keyTerms.mi: Elastic demand means buyers ignore price changes because the product is important.
keyTerms.cx: Buyers respond strongly in elastic demand, so quantity shifts more than price changes proportionally.

keyTerms.df: Close substitutes are alternative goods that make switching easier when price differences appear.
keyTerms.eg: When two similar snacks are both available, a higher price for one can shift buyers to the other.
keyTerms.mi: Close substitutes matter only after income changes, not after price changes.
keyTerms.cx: Their main role is during price comparisons because easier switching changes the quantity response.

scenario.su: A campus snack kiosk raises the price of one bottled drink while a similar drink sits nearby at nearly the same shelf height. Sales records show a sharp drop for the raised item, and the manager must decide whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
scenario.ma: Compare the sales log for the raised drink, the shelf note showing a similar nearby drink, and the price-change record for the kiosk item.

mc.q: A manager observes that one product’s quantity falls much more than its price rises, while another product changes only slightly. Which interpretation best matches the comparison?
op: Both products must be inelastic because quantity still changed.
The first product must have fewer substitutes because its quantity changed more.
The second product is elastic because its quantity changed less.
The first product has elastic demand, and the second is more inelastic.
mc.ex: Elastic demand fits when quantity changes proportionally more than price. The smaller response points toward inelastic demand, not elasticity in the second product.

mc.q: A store records a modest price increase for a snack and a much larger quantity shift toward a similar brand on the same shelf. Which explanation is best supported?
op: The snack likely has close substitutes that raise elasticity.
The quantity shift proves price elasticity is unrelated to substitutes.
The snack’s demand must be inelastic because any price rise was modest.
The snack is probably a necessity with few substitutes.
mc.ex: Close substitutes make switching easier, so demand responds more strongly to price changes. The necessity explanation conflicts with the observed shelf alternatives.

facts: A higher price raises the quantity producers are willing to supply.
Supply curves slope upward when price and quantity supplied move together.
A change in own price causes movement along the supply curve.
Changes in input costs or technology shift the entire supply curve.
Quantity supplied is a flow measured per period, not a fixed stock.

keyTerms.df: A supply curve shows how quantity supplied changes as the good's own price changes.
keyTerms.eg: A product sheet showing more units offered at a higher price traces a supply curve.
keyTerms.mi: A student may think the supply curve stays fixed whenever price changes.
keyTerms.cx: Price changes alter quantity supplied along the curve, while other changes can move the curve itself.

keyTerms.df: Quantity supplied is the amount producers offer during a specific period at a given price.
keyTerms.eg: A seller plans units offered for one market period at one price.
keyTerms.mi: A student may treat quantity supplied as the total number of goods ever available.
keyTerms.cx: The term refers to a per-period flow, not a permanent stock of goods.

keyTerms.df: Input costs are production expenses that can shift supply by changing the conditions for offering goods.
keyTerms.eg: If materials become more expensive, the supply relationship can move rather than slide.
keyTerms.mi: A student may think input costs only change the price on the same curve.
keyTerms.cx: When input costs change, the whole supply curve can shift instead of only one point moving.

scenario.su: A bakery tracks weekly bread sales and notices the posted loaf price rose while the amount offered increased. The manager also has a supplier memo showing flour costs changed and a production note about a new oven setting, and must decide whether to describe the change as movement along the supply curve or a shift.
scenario.ma: Compare the price sheet listing a higher loaf price with larger weekly quantity supplied, the supplier memo noting flour costs rose, and the production note describing a new oven setting.

mc.q: A chart shows more units offered when price rises, while the production note stays unchanged. Which interpretation best matches the relationship between supply curve and quantity supplied?
op: Input costs must have shifted the entire supply curve.
Technology changed, so the curve shifted right.
Quantity supplied is a fixed stock and cannot vary.
The higher price caused movement along the supply curve.
mc.ex: The upward relationship means a higher price raises quantity supplied along the same curve. The closest distractor is the cost-shift idea, but no input-cost change is described here.

mc.q: A manager sees unchanged price tags but hears that input costs changed and new technology was introduced before output plans were revised. What adjustment best fits the evidence?
op: The supply curve shifted because conditions other than own price changed.
Quantity supplied is a stock, so no supply adjustment is needed.
The situation describes demand, not supply, so nothing can be inferred.
Only movement along the supply curve occurred because price changed.
mc.ex: The evidence points to changes in input costs or technology, which shift supply. The closest distractor is the price-change idea, but price is unchanged, so movement along the curve is not the fit.

facts: A seventh chord adds a seventh above a triad within harmony.
Its function depends on scale degree and pull in progression.
The supertonic seventh chord acts as a terminal pre-dominant.
That supertonic sonority shows strong pull toward the dominant.
Adding a seventh to the dominant increases pull toward tonic.

keyTerms.df: A seventh chord is a triadic harmony expanded by one added seventh above the root.
keyTerms.eg: A chord built from a triad plus a seventh can sound more directed in motion.
keyTerms.mi: Any chord containing four notes is automatically a seventh chord.
keyTerms.cx: Four-note spacing alone is insufficient; the defining feature is a triad plus a seventh above it.

keyTerms.df: The supertonic seventh chord is a scale-degree specific sonority that commonly prepares dominant arrival.
keyTerms.eg: In a progression, a supertonic seventh can sit before a dominant chord with directed motion.
keyTerms.mi: The supertonic seventh functions like a final tonic arrival because it sounds stable.
keyTerms.cx: Its role is preparatory, not resting; it points forward toward the dominant instead of settling there.

keyTerms.df: Pull toward tonic is the sense that a harmony points toward tonic resolution within tonal motion.
keyTerms.eg: A dominant with an added seventh can feel more eager to resolve back home.
keyTerms.mi: Any chord that sounds bright has the same pull toward tonic.
keyTerms.cx: Brightness alone does not determine resolution tendency; tonal function depends on the chord's scale-degree role.

scenario.su: A student labels two chords in a progression: one is built on the supertonic with a seventh, and the other is a dominant seventh before the cadence. The instructor wants the labels justified from their placement and directed motion, not from note count alone.
scenario.ma: The progression trace shows the supertonic seventh moving into the dominant, then the dominant seventh resolving to tonic. The student notes one sonority has four stacked chord tones, while the other has an added seventh above a dominant triad.

mc.q: A progression shows a supertonic sonority with a seventh leading into dominant, while a four-note sonority later resolves to tonic. Which description best matches the first sonority's function in that context?
op: tonic substitute that closes the phrase
dominant prolongation that confirms tonic
median color chord that weakens motion
terminal pre-dominant that points toward dominant
mc.ex: The supertonic seventh is identified as a terminal pre-dominant with strong pull toward dominant. The tonic-substitute choice is the closest distractor, but the sonority is preparatory rather than closing.

mc.q: In a short cadence, one chord is a dominant triad with an added seventh, and the following harmony is tonic. Which reading best fits the dominant seventh's role in that progression?
op: it increases pull toward tonic
it turns into a supertonic pre-dominant
it functions chiefly as a stable resting sonority
it removes the chord's tendency to resolve
mc.ex: The added seventh on the dominant increases pull toward tonic, which suits the observed resolution. The stable resting-sonority choice is the closest distractor, but dominant sevenths are directed, not settled.

facts: Major and natural minor scales differ by ordered whole-step and half-step patterns.
The major-scale step pattern moves whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.
Natural minor includes a whole step from the seventh degree to tonic.
That raised seventh degree in natural minor is called the subtonic.
Scale-degree ordering reveals whether adjacent notes form major or natural minor patterns.

keyTerms.df: A major scale is a scale type identified by its ordered whole-step and half-step pattern.
keyTerms.eg: A pattern of whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half fits major scale.
keyTerms.mi: Any scale that sounds bright must be a major scale.
keyTerms.cx: Brightness is not the criterion; the ordered step pattern is what identifies major scale.

keyTerms.df: Natural minor is a scale type distinguished by its own ordered steps between adjacent degrees.
keyTerms.eg: A line with a whole step from the seventh degree to tonic fits natural minor.
keyTerms.mi: Natural minor must end with a half step into tonic.
keyTerms.cx: That ending belongs to another pattern; natural minor keeps a whole step into tonic.

keyTerms.df: The subtonic is the seventh degree in natural minor when it lies a whole step below tonic.
keyTerms.eg: In a natural minor line, the seventh degree above tonic functions as the subtonic.
keyTerms.mi: The subtonic is always the leading tone in minor.
keyTerms.cx: A whole step below tonic is not a leading tone; that is the subtonic in natural minor.

scenario.su: A score shows two short stepwise patterns, and you must label which one is major and which one is natural minor. One pattern ends with a half step into tonic, while the other reaches tonic by a whole step.
scenario.ma: Compare the notated adjacent steps in each pattern and the final approach to tonic. The pattern with whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half fits major scale, while the pattern with a whole step from the seventh degree to tonic shows natural minor and its subtonic.

mc.q: Two stepwise patterns are written above a tonic, and only one follows whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. Which label fits that ordered pattern best?
op: major scale
natural minor
leading tone
subtonic
mc.ex: The major-scale pattern is the ordered sequence of whole and half steps named in the facts. Natural minor is the closest distractor, but its defining detail here is the whole step from the seventh degree to tonic, not this exact pattern.

mc.q: A melody in minor reaches tonic by a whole step from its seventh degree, and the notation marks that seventh degree as the note before tonic. Which label fits that degree?
op: natural minor
subtonic
half step
major scale
mc.ex: The seventh degree a whole step below tonic is the subtonic. Natural minor is the closest distractor, but it names the scale type rather than the specific degree.
